claim: The two parts of a bipartite object have no singular form denoting just one of them: ∗damaged the lower shear. Footnote 7 marks singular trouser with %.
evidence_summary: OED shear, n.¹ sense 1.i, “One of the blades of a pair of shears”, from 1794: The upper shear is rivetted to a couple of strong standards (G. Adams, Lectures on Natural and Experimental Philosophy). A second quotation comes from Cassell’s Technical Educator (1884).
finding: A technical singular for one blade is attested, so shear deserves the % treatment footnote 7 gives trouser. The claim for slack and spectacle was not tested.
proposed_wording: and there is generally no singular form denoting just one of them: ∗torn his left slack / %damaged the lower shear / ∗cracked the right spectacle
inference: Does any bipartite plural have a singular denoting one part?

evidence.example: Sense 1.i: “One of the blades of a pair of shears”, 1794–. Quotation 1794 (G. Adams): The upper shear is rivetted to a couple of strong standards.
evidence.establishes: An edited dictionary records a singular for one part of this bipartite tool. The sense display also carries a Scottish English label; both quotations are from technical works.
evidence.locator: Meaning & use, sense 1.i. Accessed 19 November 2026 through the University of Toronto Libraries subscription.
